Allen County by the numbers

When is property tax due in Allen County, Ohio?

Allen County real estate tax is paid in two installments, normally due on the second Wednesday of February and the second Wednesday of July. The county treasurer's page lists the 2026 tax year, payable in 2027, as February 10 and July 14, 2027. Bills usually go out in January and June, though the treasurer's FAQ explains that the exact date moves with whenever the auditor delivers the calculated tax file.

A seller with sewer service should ask the closing agent to check the sewer balance along with the property tax, since both flow through the treasurer's office.

What happens if an Allen County tax payment is late?

A payment postmarked within 10 days after the due date carries a 5 percent penalty, and one postmarked later carries 10 percent. The treasurer's FAQ describes these as penalties required by state law. An owner can mail in an Application for Remission to ask for a waiver.

The treasurer also posts a warning about the mail. A postmark usually shows the day the Postal Service machinery first processed the envelope, which can be a day or more after drop-off. Because Ohio law reads the postmark date, a check mailed close to the deadline can arrive late on paper. The office suggests mailing early, asking the post office for a hand-stamped postmark, or paying in person, by card or by e-check.

How can you pay the Allen County treasurer?

The office takes cash, checks, cards and e-checks, and it is closed on federal holidays. The treasurer's counter is at 237 N Main St, Suite 123, Lima, OH 45801, and the office phone is (419) 223-8515. The treasurer's home page shows a weekday close of 4:30 p.m. while its FAQ says 4:15 p.m., so call before a deadline-day trip.

  • Online through the Search and Pay Property Taxes tab, or by phone at 1-419-765-6401.
  • In person, or at the drop box by the automatic doors outside the courthouse.
  • At Superior Credit Union or The Union Bank Company branches in the county, free of charge and open to non-customers, but only from mid-January to the February deadline and from mid-June to the July deadline.
  • By card or e-check through a third-party vendor, which adds a convenience fee: 2.40 percent (with a $2 minimum) for cards and a flat $1 for e-checks.

Two payment plans exist for owners who prefer smaller bites. The TEPP in-house escrow spreads annual taxes over 10 months, and the AUTO-Pay program pulls the exact amount from a bank account on each due date or once a year on the second Wednesday in February.

How is an Allen County tax bill figured?

The treasurer's FAQ states the method plainly: market value is multiplied by 35 percent to reach assessed value, and assessed value is multiplied by the effective tax rate for the owner's political subdivision to get gross tax. Levies take effect in the year voters approve them, but the bill for that year is payable the next year. A five-year levy approved in November of one year, for instance, shows up on the bills due the following year.

The county auditor's site has a property search and a tax calculator, and the treasurer's resources section lists tax rates, tax duplicates, school districts, cities and villages, and townships. Look up your parcel there to see your own rate, because the rate depends on the school district and village or township lines.

How do you challenge an Allen County valuation?

File a Complaint Against Valuation with the county auditor between January 1 and March 31, according to the auditor's FAQ. Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 sets the deadline as March 31 of the following year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later, and it treats a mailed complaint's postal postmark as the filing date. A private meter postmark does not count.

  • The auditor hands every complaint to the county board of revision.
  • Other parties can file a counter-complaint within 30 days of notice.
  • The board must decide an original complaint within 180 days after the last filing date.
  • While a complaint is pending, the treasurer accepts tax computed on the value you claim.
  • You must give the board all evidence you hold, or you can be barred from using it on appeal.

Destroyed or damaged property has a separate form, the Application for Valuation Deduction. The auditor says to file as soon as possible because refunds for prior years are not issued.

Which tax reductions can an Allen County homeowner claim?

The auditor's FAQ names three programs. The Owner Occupancy Credit, a 2.5 percent rollback, applies to a primary residence. The Homestead reduction covers owners who are 65 or older or who are permanently and totally disabled, and the application goes to the auditor, with postmarks accepted. CAUV lowers valuation for commercial farmland.

These credits matter when you sell, because the buyer's statement of value under section 319.202 asks whether the seller's taxes were reduced. Ask the auditor for the credits currently attached to your parcel.

Who owes the tax when an Allen County house sells?

The auditor's FAQ says taxes follow ownership and are usually prorated at closing, and that the auditor does not prorate. If closing skips the step, the new owner is the one billed. Taxes are charged on the property as it stood on January 1, so a parcel split mid-year is billed whole until someone requests a tax split. After a transfer it takes a year for the previous owner's name to clear from the treasurer's system, which does not change who must pay.

At transfer, the auditor's FAQ quotes a conveyance fee of $3.00 per thousand of the purchase price and a $.50 per parcel transfer charge. A title company will normally add both to the settlement statement.

What does the Allen County economy mean for housing?

Allen County has about 100,881 residents, and in 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau put median household income at $64,038 and median gross rent at $922. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,240, and those without one $535. Workers commute 18.7 minutes on average, and 60.7 percent of residents 16 or older are in the labor force. The county counted 2,239 employer establishments and 44,251 jobs in 2023, plus retail sales of $20,786 per resident in 2022.

Those QuickFacts describe the county as a whole. The auditor's property search is the place to see what your own street's neighbors are assessed at.

More questions about Allen County, OH Property Tax Guide

When is the second half of property tax due in Allen County?

The posted due date for the 2026 tax year is Wednesday, July 14, 2027, and the first half is due Wednesday, February 10, 2027. In general both fall on the second Wednesday of their month.

What is the penalty for paying Allen County property tax late?

It is 5 percent if the payment is postmarked within 10 days after the due date and 10 percent after that. The treasurer's FAQ also offers a remission application to request a waiver.

Can I pay Allen County property tax with a credit card?

Yes. Cards and e-checks are taken online, by phone at 1-419-765-6401 and in the office, with the vendor's fee of 2.40 percent (at least $2) for cards or $1 for an e-check.

How do I appeal my Allen County property value?

File a Complaint Against Valuation with the Allen County Auditor between January 1 and March 31. The auditor then presents it to the county board of revision.

Who pays the property tax when I sell my Allen County home?

Taxes follow ownership and are usually prorated at closing. The auditor's office does not prorate them, so ask your closing agent to settle the split on the statement.

Belmont County by the numbers

Where is Belmont County, Ohio, and who lives there?

Belmont County fills a stretch of Ohio's eastern border, where the Ohio River separates it from West Virginia. Wikipedia lists 541.27 square miles of area, most of it low rolling hills cut by creeks such as Captina and McMahon. St. Clairsville is the county seat, and Martins Ferry is the largest city.

The county was created on September 7, 1801, and has kept its present boundaries since 1813. Coal, the National Road and the river trade shaped it early. Bellaire counted 15 glass factories by 1881 and was called the Glass City. Today the county is part of the Wheeling metropolitan area.

The 2020 census counted 66,497 people. The 2025 estimate is 64,434, which is 3.1 percent lower. Almost 25 percent of residents are 65 or older, which bears on the homestead credit discussed below. Public high schools sit in Bellaire, Bridgeport, Martins Ferry, Saint Clairsville and Shadyside, and Buckeye Local and Union Local have high schools of their own.

What do Census figures say about Belmont County homes?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for Belmont County shows a modest, owner-heavy market. Survey years are 2020 to 2024 except where a bullet says otherwise.

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $154,900.
  • Owner-occupied housing unit rate: 73.6 percent, across 27,195 households.
  • Median gross rent: $793 a month.
  • Median household income: $57,017, with 15.1 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Mean commute: 25.1 minutes.
  • Permits issued during 2025: 2.

The county auditor's own site lists 76,512 parcels. Ask the treasurer for the balance on a given parcel number.

Which Belmont County offices handle property tax?

A seller can finish every step inside the courthouse at 101 West Main Street, St. Clairsville. One office sets the value, one sends the bill, and one files the deed.

  • Auditor. Sets values, takes board of revision complaints and endorses deeds. The main line is 740-699-2130, real estate is 740-699-2132, and the deed transfer desk is 740-699-2136. Walk-in service runs weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30.
  • Treasurer. Mails the bills and takes payment. Phone 740-699-2145 on weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30.
  • Recorder. Files deeds and mortgages and, in the recorder's words, looks after more than 220 years of county land records. The office does not run title searches.

The treasurer can give the rate of taxation for your district, which varies with the school and village levies.

When are Belmont County property taxes due?

Real estate tax comes in two installments, mailed in January and June. By the treasurer's FAQ, the due dates usually fall in the third week of February and of July, unless the bill says otherwise.

Source: Belmont County Treasurer, treasurer FAQ and auditor timeline.

A postmark counts as timely, and the treasurer suggests carrying the envelope into the post office so it gets stamped. A secure drop box sits on the left side of the courthouse front stairs and is open only during the January and February and June and July collection periods. Cash does not go in the box.

Ohio bills taxes one year behind. Ohio taxes run in arrears, so a bill arriving in 2026 covers tax year 2025.

What happens when a Belmont County tax payment is late?

The county adds a penalty first and interest later. Under Ohio Revised Code 323.121, a ten percent penalty attaches to an unpaid half, and interest on older delinquent tax runs at the rate set under section 5703.47.

The treasurer's FAQ is blunt on two points. A missing bill is no excuse, since the owner is responsible under section 323.13. A request to remit the penalty can still be filed when something outside the owner's control got in the way, such as hospitalization, a prolonged illness or the death of an immediate family member.

Owners who are behind should call 740-699-2145 and ask about payment options. The statute recognizes delinquent tax contracts, and while one stays in effect no ten percent penalty is added to the covered first-half taxes after the second-half collection period.

If back taxes go unpaid long enough, the parcel can reach tax foreclosure. The auditor's office has run forfeited land sales for parcels that failed to sell at foreclosure. The opening bid equals current taxes plus court costs, and the winning bidder pays the deed, conveyance and recording fees. Selling the house before that point keeps the proceeds with the owner.

How do you challenge a Belmont County valuation?

A valuation complaint is filed at the auditor's office. Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 gives owners until the later of two dates: the last day of March following the tax year, or the day first-half collection closes. The treasurer's FAQ tells owners March 31.

The hearing notice must reach the owner at least ten days beforehand. A mailed complaint is judged by its United States postmark, and a private meter mark does not count. Taxing bodies such as a school board can file their own complaints or counter-complaints, so the district may appear at the hearing.

Belmont County's latest reappraisal ran on this path:

  • January 2022: the Ohio Department of Taxation ordered the reappraisal for tax year 2024.
  • April 2022: data mailers went to every property with a dwelling.
  • Summer and fall 2024: informal reviews with owners.
  • October 2024: final values went to the state.
  • January 2025: bills with the new values were mailed, and the complaint window ran January 1 to March 31, 2025.

Ohio generally limits an owner to one complaint per interim period, with listed exceptions such as an improvement added to the property or a 15 percent swing in occupancy. Ask the auditor which year Belmont County sits in before filing.

Which tax breaks can a Belmont County owner claim?

The homestead exemption is the main one. The Ohio Department of Taxation publishes the tax year 2026 table: $29,700 of market value shielded for low-income seniors and disabled owners, $59,400 for disabled veterans, and a $41,000 income limit on the first group.

Send the application to the auditor before the year ends, because the credit is tied to the calendar year. A denied application can go to the board of revision on form DTE 106B, filed within 60 days of the notice. The treasurer's site also carries the homestead application for seniors, disabled residents and surviving spouses.

The credit does not pass with the deed, so the buyer qualifies on his or her own. That is why the deed paperwork asks about it, as the next section explains.

How is tax handled when a Belmont County house sells?

The auditor's endorsement is the first step on a deed. Section 319.202 has the buyer or a representative file a statement of value. That filing must say the seller was asked about any homestead or owner-occupancy tax cut on the house. If the seller answered yes, a sworn estimate of the cut is attached.

The auditor's value-statement fee comes from section 319.54(G)(3): a flat dollar or ten cents per hundred, whichever is higher. The same section lists exempt transfers, among them gifts within a family. Section 322.02 also lets a county levy a deed transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100. Ask the deed transfer desk at 740-699-2136 for Belmont County's current conveyance rate.

A seller who still gets a bill after closing is told to review the closing papers and then contact the title company, banker or agent. Unpaid tax that the closing statement never addressed can stay with the owner. Pay off or prorate the bill at the table.

More questions about Belmont County, OH Property Tax Guide

Does Belmont County collect the second half in July?

Yes. Expect the second half around the third week of July. The 2025 tax year bills fell due on Friday, February 20, 2026 (first half) and Friday, July 24, 2026 (second half). Mailing happens in January and in June or early July, and the printed date on your bill controls.

Who values a house in Belmont County?

The county auditor values every parcel, and the auditor's office lists 76,512 of them. The treasurer only bills and collects. Complaints about value are filed with the auditor, whose office serves as the board's secretary.

How steep is the Belmont County late penalty?

A payment inside the ten-day grace window draws 5 percent. Later than that, the treasurer's notice puts it at 10 percent of what is still owed for the current year. The statute also adds interest on older delinquent tax. A penalty remission request is possible for circumstances beyond your control.

Can I sell a Belmont County house with back taxes?

Yes. Phone 740-699-2145 for the payoff number, and the title company can pay it off at closing. A sale ahead of any tax foreclosure keeps the decision with you, where a forfeited land sale ends it.

Can the buyer keep my homestead reduction?

No. The credit belongs to the qualifying owner who lives in the home. The deed paperwork asks the seller about any reduction. A buyer who qualifies must apply separately. Applications go to the auditor, with a December 31 cutoff.

Butler County by the numbers

Where is Butler County, Ohio, and which communities does it include?

Butler County lies in southwestern Ohio, with Hamilton County to its south, Montgomery County to the northeast and Indiana to the west. Hamilton is the seat and the largest city. Wikipedia gives 470 square miles of area, mostly the valleys of the Great Miami and Little Miami rivers. It was formed in 1803 from part of Hamilton County and is named for General Richard Butler.

The county has seven cities: Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown, Monroe, Oxford, Sharonville and Trenton. Five villages and thirteen civil townships fill in the rest, among them West Chester, Liberty, Lemon and Reily. Miami University was chartered in 1809 on a township the legislature set aside for a college. Sixteen school districts have territory here, including Lakota, Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown and Talawanda.

The 2020 census counted 390,357 residents, which ranks Butler seventh among Ohio counties. By July 2025 the Bureau estimated 400,128. A property tax bill in this county therefore depends heavily on which of the many taxing districts a house falls into.

What do Census figures show for Butler County homeowners?

The Census Bureau QuickFacts table for Butler County shows a larger and pricier market than its eastern Ohio neighbors. The 2020 to 2024 figures are:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $258,500.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 69.9 percent among 146,822 households.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,665 with a mortgage, $619 without.
  • Median gross rent: $1,135.
  • Median household income: $81,590.
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,021, against 158,143 housing units.

The estimate for July 2025 is 2.5 percent above the April 2020 base.

How much did the 2026 reappraisal raise Butler County values?

The auditor reports a median residential and agricultural increase of 19 percent for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, and a median 20 percent for commercial and industrial property. The state Department of Tax Equalization approved the value abstract on June 25. The office adds that its sales ratio sits near 90 percent of full market value.

Source: Butler County Auditor news release, which lists every jurisdiction.

The release stresses that voted levies move a bill more than value does. It names a new countywide 2-mill developmental disabilities levy at about $70 per $100,000 of value, and a 4.49-mill Fairfield Township fire levy at about $157 per $100,000. Those are the office's own figures. The release says new state laws blunt the effect of higher values, and the auditor's homepage points to an inflation cap credit on second-half bills under House Bill 186.

Ohio's cycle brings a reappraisal every six years and a triennial update halfway between. Butler County's schedule lists 2026 as the latest reappraisal and 2032 as the next, with updates in 2023 and 2029.

How is a Butler County property tax bill figured?

The treasurer explains that taxable value is 35 percent of the auditor's fair market value. The auditor multiplies that taxable value by the total mill rate and divides by 1,000. Levies and special assessments are added, then reduction credits come off.

  • Parcel numbers. A real estate parcel is a letter followed by 13 numbers, and about 160,000 parcels exist in the county.
  • Taxing districts. The treasurer counts 66 separate districts, so a house in Hamilton and one in Liberty Township can carry different rates.
  • Reduction factors. A levy cannot raise more than it did when voters passed it, so the state applies a reduction factor to the gross rate.
  • Credits. The non-business credit and the owner-occupancy credit apply only to levies in place before the November 2013 election. Homestead is a separate reduction for qualifying seniors, disabled owners and veterans.

Special assessments for items like street paving or weed removal also show on the bill and go back to the government that levied them.

What are the Butler County tax due dates?

The treasurer collects twice a year. The first half is typically due in mid to late February and the second half in early August, and the printed bill carries the exact date. The 2025 second half was mailed on July 20, 2026, and was due Wednesday, August 19, 2026. The treasurer's number for a missing bill is (513) 887-3181.

Taxes in Ohio are paid in arrears, which makes a 2026 payment cover tax year 2025. A payment more than ten days late draws a 10 percent penalty. Paid in full within the first ten days, the penalty is 5 percent, as the treasurer's timeline explains under section 323.121.

Interest is added twice a year. For older balances it starts the first of the month after the second-half due date, and a second charge lands December 1 on everything still unpaid. An owner can file an Application for Remission of Penalty, but the law allows remission only in limited cases.

What is the route to appeal a Butler County valuation?

Value disputes go before the Board of Revision, a three-member panel: the auditor, the treasurer and one county commissioner. The auditor says the board reviews values, not the amount of tax owed. The filing window is January 1 to March 31, and an owner generally files once in each three-year valuation period.

Filing steps, as the office describes them:

  • Complete DTE Form 1, Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, with any supporting documentation.
  • Submit it through the office's online vendor, by email to bor@bcohio.gov, or by mail.
  • Expect a Notice of Hearing by email or certified mail.
  • Allow three to four weeks after the hearing for the Notice of Result.

A request to cut market value by $50,000 or more can draw a counter-complaint from another eligible party such as a school board. After a decision, the owner has 30 days from the mailing date to appeal to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas, and must tell the board of revision too. The 2026 values open for complaint in January and close March 31 of the following year.

What do Butler County sellers pay at the auditor and recorder?

The deed visits the auditor first and the recorder second. The auditor's FAQ prints the conveyance fee as $3.00 per thousand of the price, with the price rounded up to the next hundred, and $.50 for each parcel. Real estate has a $3.00 minimum plus the parcel fee. Payment is by cash or check made out to the Butler County Auditor.

DTE Form 100 goes with an ordinary sale and Form 100EX with an exempt transfer. The legal description must be attached, and the auditor asks owners to have the Engineer's Office at 513-867-5744 preapprove it before submitting. Transfers can come by mail, in person or by e-file.

  • $4.00 per reference for a satisfaction or release.

The sheet also calls for a parcel number on each deed, a self-addressed stamped return envelope, and a prepared-by statement when the notary is in Ohio. Turnaround is listed as 24 hours. The recorder's office is at 130 High Street in Hamilton, and the fee sheet gives (513) 887-3192.

Residential and agricultural values rose by a median of 19 percent, and commercial and industrial by 20 percent. Changes differ by place, from a median 39 percent in Lemon Township to 12 percent in the city of Fairfield. New voted levies affect the bill as much as value does.

Can I appeal my Butler County valuation every year?

Generally no. An owner may file once in each three-year valuation period, with some exceptions the statute lists. The window opens January 1 and shuts March 31, and DTE Form 1 is the form to use.

What conveyance fee applies to a Butler County sale?

The auditor prints $3.00 per thousand of the price (rounded up to the next hundred) and $.50 per parcel. Checks go to the Butler County Auditor. Ask the auditor at 513-887-3154 about exemptions that call for Form 100EX.

Clark County by the numbers

Which Clark County offices set values and send tax bills?

Springfield's A.B. Graham Building, 31 North Limestone Street, houses both offices that touch your tax bill. The auditor (937-521-1860) decides what each parcel is worth. The treasurer (937-521-1832) prints, mails and collects the bills.

On its own page the treasurer's office lists annual collections of $135 million in real estate tax and $275,000 in manufactured home tax. Each bill stacks levies from several local taxing bodies.

For the levy breakdown on your district, ask the treasurer for the yearly rate sheet. The property tax page has a link to it, and the counter hands out paper copies.

The treasurer's main page links to online payment. Written notices, such as a change of mailing address, go to the treasurer at P.O. Box 1305, Springfield, OH 45501-1305.

How often does Clark County reappraise homes?

Clark County's auditor follows a six year reappraisal cycle with a sales-based triennial update halfway through. The auditor's triennial update FAQ separates the two: a reappraisal includes an inspection of each property, and an update looks only at sales. Its 2022 round drew on 2019, 2020 and 2021 sales and priced homes as they stood on January 1, 2022.

The FAQ describes a mass appraisal done by a hired contractor across more than 50,000 residential parcels. It lists location, lot size, age, style, square footage, construction quality, foundation, outbuildings and condition as the factors that feed a value. It also explains the arithmetic behind a bill: appraised value, then 35 percent of it, then the voted levies, yields the gross tax. Most rates are adjusted yearly so each levy raises what it raised the year before.

What are the Clark County payment dates and late charges?

A year of tax comes in two installments. The treasurer's page for the 2025 tax year names February 27, 2026 for the first installment and August 7, 2026 for the second, both now in the past. Later cycles carry their own dates, so rely on the bill itself. Mailing happens 20 to 25 days ahead of each deadline, and the office stresses that never receiving a bill does not cancel the tax or the penalties.

Mailing a check late in the window carries a trap. Section 323.12 accepts a Postal Service postmark dated by the final day, and rejects a postage meter stamp from a private machine.

Can you spread Clark County property tax into monthly payments?

The treasurer's escrow program converts each half-year bill into equal monthly prepayments. Participants sign an agreement and get coupons showing an estimated amount, though any amount is accepted on any day. Cash, check, money order and ACH debit all work, and the page says the program costs nothing to use.

  • Mail the Escrow Program Form to P.O. Box 1305, Springfield, OH 45501-1305, or email it to treasurer@clarkcountyohio.gov.

  • Report a new mailing address in writing, since a bill sent to an old address still counts as issued.

Anyone listing a house should ask the treasurer how a prepaid balance is handled at closing.

How can an owner contest a Clark County valuation?

The complaint form goes to the county auditor, and section 5715.19 sets the cutoff: March 31 of the year after the tax year, or the day first-half collection closes if that falls later. Postal postmarks count as the filing date for mailed forms. Owners, their spouses and certain retained professionals can sign.

  • The auditor forwards each complaint to the Clark County Board of Revision, which has 180 days after the filing deadline to hear and decide it.
  • The auditor's FAQ puts the burden on the owner and names a recent arm's length sale, of your home or a similar one, as the strongest proof.
  • During the wait you may tender tax based on the value you claimed, and the treasurer must accept it.
  • One complaint per interim period is the limit unless something changed afterward, such as a sale, a casualty loss or a major addition.

The FAQ recommends starting with the auditor's informal review. Section 5715.19(G) also requires a complainant to give the Board of Revision all evidence in their possession. Anything held back may be barred if the case moves on to the Board of Tax Appeals or the common pleas court, unless good cause is shown.

Which relief programs cut a Clark County tax bill?

The homestead exemption leads the list. The state's tax department FAQ describes a credit for owners aged 65 or more, owners who are permanently and totally disabled, and some surviving spouses. In tax year 2026 it equals the tax charged on $29,700 of value, with a $41,000 income ceiling. Disabled veterans see $59,400 and face no income test.

  • Form DTE 105A (or DTE 105I for veterans) goes to the Clark County Auditor, due December 31 of the credit year.
  • Applicants turn 65 by the end of that year and must have owned and lived in the house since January 1.
  • A denial can be taken to the Board of Revision on DTE 106B inside 60 days.

House Bill 96, signed in June 2025, lets county commissioners add a matching local option. The auditor can say whether Clark County adopted one.

What happens to unpaid taxes when a Clark County house sells?

A balance stays with the parcel, and the buyer's title search will surface it. Call 937-521-1832 for a payoff figure, hand it to whoever runs the closing, and have it settled out of the proceeds. The penalty and interest steps in the table above continue until the day of payment.

The deed paperwork adds one more tax question. Section 319.202 has the buyer record what the seller says about whether the current or previous year's taxes will be reduced under the homestead or owner-occupancy rules. Know your own answer before closing day, because a yes means a sworn estimate of the reduction travels with the deed.

What do the numbers say about Clark County homeowners?

West central Ohio's Clark County spans 403 square miles around the seat, Springfield. Wikipedia names two cities, Springfield and New Carlisle, and puts the rural share of 2020 residents at 25.4 percent. From Census QuickFacts:

  • Households (2020 to 2024): 55,975, averaging 2.37 people.

Call 937-521-1832, the number the property tax page prints for bill questions. The office is in the Graham Building on North Limestone Street.

August 7, 2026, for the second half. February 27, 2026 was the first-half date. A 5 percent penalty and then a 10 percent penalty followed each one.

The Clark County Auditor receives it and passes it to the Board of Revision. March 31 of the next year is the cutoff, unless first-half collection closes later.

How is a Clark County bill calculated from market value?

Which Batavia offices handle a Clermont County tax bill?

The auditor values the parcel and the treasurer takes the payment. Both work out of the county building in Batavia, and the auditor answers questions at 513-732-7150 on weekdays until 4:30 p.m.

Clermont ranks as Ohio's eighth oldest county. It borders the Ohio River, covers roughly 452 square miles of land, and seats its government in Batavia while Milford is the biggest city. Villages include Bethel, Felicity, Moscow, New Richmond, Owensville and Williamsburg, plus fourteen townships. A house in West Clermont territory and one in Williamsburg can sit under very different school levies, so the parcel number matters more than the street address.

For payment questions the treasurer's number is 513-732-7254. Look the parcel up in the auditor's property search first so you have the number ready.

How is a Clermont County house valued for tax?

The auditor sets fair market value and bills on 35% of it. Nearly 95,000 parcels sit in the county. A full reappraisal runs every six years, a midpoint update lands in between, and new construction is picked up annually.

Field appraisers drive clearly marked auditor vehicles and note additions, recent sales, damage and teardowns. A yellow door card means they stopped by and nobody answered. A seller who finished a basement or removed a garage should assume that change will show in the next value.

  • Value tracks the market, not the original purchase price.
  • Rates come from votes on levies, so a valuation complaint cannot lower a rate.
  • Bills run a year in arrears: what you pay in 2026 belongs to tax year 2025.

What are the Clermont County payment dates and penalties?

Each year has a first-half and a second-half installment. The joint auditor and treasurer notice put the first-half 2026 deadline at Friday, February 13, 2026, which has passed. Payment options listed by the county are online, by phone, by mail, or the drop box outside 101 E. Main Street.

The Revised Code sets December 31 and June 20 as its default dates in section 323.12 and lets a county extend them through section 323.17. A letter counts if the U.S. Postal Service stamped it by the last day; a postage meter stamp does not.

Section 323.121 adds a ten percent charge on an unpaid installment and halves it when the full amount comes in within ten days. Older unpaid balances pick up interest at the rate section 5703.47 prescribes.

Why did Clermont County second-half bills slip?

House Bill 186 created an inflation cap credit, and Clermont had to rebuild its second-half calculations to apply it. The auditor's list of school districts touched by the change reads Bethel-Tate, Blanchester, Clermont Northeastern, Felicity-Franklin, Goshen, Little Miami, West Clermont, Williamsburg and Great Oaks JVS.

The January 22, 2026 notice from the auditor and treasurer told owners they could pay first-half taxes alone and that overpayments would be refunded after several weeks. Lenders were asked to hold their escrow payments. For a seller, the lesson is practical: get a payoff figure that reflects the credits instead of reusing last year's second-half amount.

The auditor's fact sheet pairs House Bill 186 with House Bills 124, 129, 309 and 335, which affect valuation procedure, the school 20-mill floor, budget commission oversight and inside millage. Most of their effects start with tax year 2026 bills paid in 2027.

Six property tax measures were listed for the November 3, 2026 ballot, among them an 8.4-mill continuing fire and EMS levy in Batavia Township and a 5.48-mill renewal for Bethel-Tate Local Schools. The auditor's levy calculator multiplies the full voted millage by the tax year 2025 value and does not apply any reduction factor the state may certify later.

When can a Clermont County owner contest the value?

Complaints against valuation are accepted from January 1 through March 31 on the Board of Revision's form. Send it electronically, mail it to 101 E. Main St., Batavia, Ohio 45103, hand it in, or email the address the auditor lists for appeals. Each owner gets one filing in a three-year stretch, and the filing opens a legal proceeding.

Revised Code 5715.19(A)(1) sets the cutoff at March 31 of the ensuing tax year or the close of first-half collection, whichever falls later. The board is the auditor as secretary, the treasurer and a commissioner, and each may send a staff member. Comparable local sales make up the best exhibit.

The board never touches a levy or a penalty. A penalty question goes to the treasurer.

Which reductions follow a Clermont County property into a sale?

Homestead, the owner occupancy credit and the one-time credit under House Bill 479 are the three to know about.

New applicants after January 1, 2014 must report Ohio adjusted gross income below $41,000. The deadline is December 31. A veteran who is 100 percent disabled from service can claim $56,000 where the standard figure is $28,000.
  • Owner occupancy credit: any owner who lived in the house as a primary residence on January 1 may apply, and the application often rides along with the deed.
  • One-time credit: House Bill 479 sends roughly $450 to $500 to Homestead recipients on tax year 2026 bills issued in 2027. The auditor's site set December 31, 2026 as the last day to become eligible.

A seller who held the Homestead reduction in the current or prior tax year must file Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property, DTE 101, with the deed. Farmland under agricultural valuation uses DTE 102.

With about 84,955 households and 2.46 people in each, the county has a steady base of family homes. Ask the auditor how the median value compares with your parcel before deciding whether a complaint is worth the effort.

What should an owner with unpaid Clermont County tax do before listing?

Call the treasurer on 513-732-7254 for the balance by parcel number and ask whether a delinquent tax contract exists. While a valid contract stays in effect, section 323.121 stops the ten percent charge and interest from building, and a void contract revives them.

Foreclosure and tax sale auctions are listed by the sheriff on 513-732-7087, and foreclosure suits are filed through the clerk of courts, 513-732-7560. Give the title company a head start by requesting payoff letters from the treasurer and each lender early.

Thirty-five percent. The auditor appraises the parcel at fair market value and the voted levies for that school district and township then apply to the 35% figure.

Only once in three years. A complaint runs on a January 1 to March 31 window and speaks to value alone, not to rates or late charges.

Yes. A seller who received the Homestead reduction in the current or prior tax year files DTE 101 alongside the DTE 100 conveyance form.

The treasurer, at 513-732-7254. The auditor, at 513-732-7150, covers values, Homestead and the owner occupancy credit.

It affected the tax year 2025 second-half bills. Ask the treasurer for the due date printed on your parcel, because revised dates were announced separately from the February 13, 2026 first-half deadline.

What is Columbiana County like for a house owner, and who sends the tax bill?

Columbiana County sits on the eastern edge of Ohio, with Pennsylvania on its east line, the Ohio River and Jefferson and Carroll counties to the south, Carroll and Stark counties to the west and Mahoning County to the north. It covers about 534 square miles in eighteen townships. Lisbon is the county seat and Salem is the largest city, and the county forms part of Appalachian Ohio.

The county auditor, at 105 S. Market Street in Lisbon, sets values and takes deeds for transfer; the number is 330-424-9515. The treasurer collects the tax and answers at 330-424-9514. Cash payments are taken at the counter between eight and four on weekdays. The recorder, at 330-424-9517, files the deed after the auditor has processed it.

East Liverpool was home to what the county's own account and Wikipedia describe as the largest pottery industry in the world, and the county's river towns carry that industrial history. Salem, Wellsville, East Palestine and Columbiana are other places a seller might name on a deed.

What dates does the Columbiana County treasurer post for tax payments?

Bills go out twice a year, usually in January and July, and Ohio bills a year behind. The treasurer's home page lists tentative 2027 dates: March 5, 2027 for first-half 2026 taxes and July 30, 2027 for second-half 2026 taxes. Treat those as the dates to confirm before closing a sale in either window.

Mail that carries a postmark from the due date or earlier is treated as on time. The treasurer prints a 5% penalty for payments made within ten days after the due date and 10% after that, and delinquent accounts add interest at a rate the Ohio Tax Commissioner sets each year. The statute behind the split is section 323.121, which waives half the penalty when full payment arrives inside ten days.

  • Cash, checks, money orders and cashier's checks are taken at the counter. Do not mail cash.
  • Online payment runs through a provider that charges 2.95% on cards with a $2.00 minimum, 2.50% per transaction on ACH, and 2.95% plus $0.95 for a card payment by phone, as the treasurer prints them.
  • For a paid receipt by mail, return the whole bill with a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

How does Columbiana County value property?

Every six years the auditor hires a professional appraisal firm to set market value. Between those, the Ohio Department of Taxation looks at sales and economic factors every three years, and the auditor adjusts values to match. A house worth more after a reappraisal does not guarantee a higher bill, because voters decide levies and the second factor in the treasurer's explanation is the ballot box.

Columbiana County government collects almost nothing from real estate tax. The treasurer's site says the county takes only a 0.2 mill for debt retirement after the commissioners chose to waive a 2 mill levy and rely on sales tax. So a bill in Salem or Lisbon is made up mostly of school, township, city or village, library and voted special levies.

If a mortgage servicer pays the tax from escrow, tell the treasurer in writing when the loan is paid off or refinanced. The office states that a lender must notify it of changes in writing, and the office asks anyone who should have received a bill and did not to call at once.

What options does a Columbiana County owner have to challenge a valuation?

An owner who thinks a valuation is wrong can use the county Board of Revision, the Ohio Department of Taxation, or Common Pleas Court. The treasurer's FAQ points to a Board of Revision complaint filed by March 31, processed through the auditor's office at 330-424-9515. The statute, section 5715.19, can allow a later cutoff when first-half collection closes after March 31.

A late-fee complaint is a separate paper. The treasurer's office handles requests to remove a penalty; call 330-424-9514 for the form and write down why the late charge should not apply.

Which credits and special valuations apply in Columbiana County?

The treasurer's page on real estate credits describes four programs, and the auditor takes every application.

  • 10% rollback: a long-standing reduction for residential real estate not used in a business.
  • 2.5% rollback: for a homestead, meaning the dwelling plus up to one acre, with an application certifying primary residence.
  • Homestead exemption: for homeowners 65 or older and those permanently and totally disabled, for a dwelling and up to one acre. Ask the auditor for the current income limit and filing window, since both have changed over the years.
  • Current agricultural use value: land with ten acres in commercial farming, or fewer than ten acres averaging at least $2,500 of yearly gross farm income, after three years of qualifying use. When land leaves the program, a charge equal to the extra tax over the previous three years applies.

Timber land run under state forestry rules may be taxed at half the local rate. A buyer taking over farm acreage should find out whether the parcel is enrolled before agreeing on a price.

Nearly one resident in four is 65 or older, so Homestead and the 2.5% rollback matter to many owners. The median home value of $151,600 and median gross rent of $756 both run well below the figures Census reports for Clermont County.

What if a Columbiana County owner is behind on tax and wants to sell?

A delinquent owner can set up a five-pay contract at the treasurer's office. The delinquent amount is split into five equal installments over two and a half years, and current taxes must still be paid on time throughout. Missing an installment voids the contract and foreclosure continues.

Section 323.121 stops penalty and interest while a valid contract stays in effect, so a sale can close with the contract balance paid at the table. Request the parcel's payoff from the treasurer and let the title company re-verify it shortly before closing.

A deed in this county goes to the auditor on the state's DTE 100 conveyance form before it reaches the recorder. The recorder's fees follow Revised Code sections 317.32 and 317.36, which split the basic fee equally between the recording fee and the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, with an optional county preservation charge on top.

The treasurer prints 5% for payments made within ten days after the due date and 10% after that. Interest is added on delinquent accounts at a rate the Ohio Tax Commissioner sets.

Can I pay a delinquent Columbiana County bill in installments?

Yes. A five-pay contract divides the delinquency into five equal installments over about two and a half years. Current taxes must stay paid, and one missed installment voids the contract.

File a complaint with the Board of Revision by March 31 through the auditor's office. Appeals can also go to the Ohio Department of Taxation or Common Pleas Court.

Who runs property tax in Cuyahoga County?

Three pieces of the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office matter to a property owner. The Appraisal department values every parcel, the Board of Revision hears complaints about those values, and the Treasurer's Office bills the real estate tax and invests the revenue. The Fiscal Officer's department page also lists Real Property for credits and charges, a Budget Commission that sets tax rates, Delinquent Tax Outreach, and a Transfer and Recording office for property records. Recorded documents are available from 1810 forward.

Everything sits at the Cuyahoga County Administrative Building, 2079 East 9th Street in Cleveland. The county's property FAQ places Transfer and Recording on the 4th floor, Appraisal on the 3rd floor, the Treasurer on the 1st floor and the Board of Revision on the 2nd, and gives 216-443-7420 as the number for land records, appraisals and the Fiscal Office.

When and how is Cuyahoga County property tax paid?

Real estate tax is billed twice a year and in arrears, one year behind. The Treasurer's Pay Your Taxes page says taxes accrued in 2025 are due in 2026, in mid-February and mid-August. Manufactured home tax is billed for the current year, with payments due in early March and late August. Owners can sign up for EasyPay to prepay future bills or for E-Billing to receive bills by email or text.

Way to payWhat the Treasurer prints

The Treasurer warns mail payers that a postmark shows when the post office machinery processed the envelope, not necessarily the day it was mailed. Because Ohio law relies on the postmark, people paying near a due date are urged to allow extra time, ask for a hand-stamped postmark at the counter, or use another payment method.

What if a Cuyahoga County owner falls behind on the tax?

Ohio Revised Code 323.121 puts a ten percent penalty on the unpaid balance of a late half and adds interest on delinquent taxes at the rate set under section 5703.47. The penalty drops by half when the whole amount comes in within ten days of the deadline. A valid delinquent tax contract stops further interest while it stays in force, and it becomes void if the owner breaks it.

The Treasurer's outreach calendar advertises Last Chance Payment Plan classes for owners who are seeking a third delinquent tax contract, offered online and at the Financial Empowerment Center at 2079 East 9th Street. The Fiscal Officer's department list also names Delinquent Tax Outreach as the unit that helps the Prosecutor and Treasurer collect overdue tax. An owner who wants to sell a house with a balance should phone the Treasurer for the amount owed and ask whether a payment contract is in place, so the title company has the full picture.

How does a Cuyahoga County owner appeal a valuation?

By lodging a complaint with the Cuyahoga County Board of Revision during the window that opens each January 1 and shuts on March 31. The Board's page says the tax year 2025 filing period has closed and the next one runs from January 1, 2027 through March 31, 2027. The county's property FAQ adds that a complaint must claim over-valuation, under-valuation, discriminatory valuation, illegal valuation or an incorrect determination of use.

The people who may file are broader than most owners expect. The FAQ lists any owner of taxable real property in the county, the commissioners, the prosecutor, the treasurer, any school board in the county, and the mayor or legislative authority of a municipality with land in the county. Cuyahoga was reappraised in 2024 under Ohio's six-year cycle, and the Fiscal Office page notes that a higher valuation does not by itself mean a higher tax bill.

A residential owner has to back up an opinion of value. The Fiscal Office lists the kinds of evidence the board expects:

  • A full appraisal report completed in the last calendar year
  • Dated photographs showing the property's existing condition
  • Certified contractor estimates for repairs
  • A purchase agreement with its closing statement
  • Certified new construction costs from the builder

Phone the board at 216-443-7195, and its office, on the second floor at 2079 East Ninth Street, keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30. Each complaint is set for a hearing, so the owner arrives with the evidence in hand.

Which tax credits and protections does Cuyahoga County offer?

The Fiscal Office links four resources to its reappraisal page: the homestead exemption, an owner occupancy credit, a military deferment under which property taxes can be deferred, and Property Alerts to protect owners from deed fraud. Each carries its own state form or sign-up, so ask the Fiscal Office which ones fit a house you own but do not live in.

The Fiscal Office's reappraisal page also stresses that an owner contesting value must produce documents, not just a figure. That applies to sellers who bought recently, since the purchase agreement and closing statement are on the evidence list.

When a house sells, the grantor pays the auditor-side conveyance fee under ORC 319.54, set at $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is more. Section 319.202 has the buyer file a statement of value, and any county transfer tax is added. In Cuyahoga County that step runs through the Fiscal Office's Transfer and Recording unit ahead of the recorded copy.

What makes Cuyahoga County different for a seller?

Cuyahoga is a large urban county on the southern shore of Lake Erie. Wikipedia gives its area as 1,246 square miles, of which 457 are land and 788 are water, and calls it the second largest county in Ohio by area. The Cuyahoga River divides it, and part of Cuyahoga Valley National Park lies in the southeast. Lawmakers created the county in 1807, it was organized on May 1, 1810, and Cleveland had been picked as its seat in 1809. Lake, Geauga, Summit, Medina, Lorain and Portage counties touch its borders.

Census QuickFacts estimates 1,232,925 residents for July 1, 2025, which is 2.5% under the 2020 base. The housing side reads:

  • 616,777 housing units, 554,551 households
  • 59.4% of homes owner-occupied
  • A typical owned home worth $195,400 in the 2020 to 2024 figures
  • Rents running at a median of $1,060 a month
  • Median household income of $64,468
  • 1,896 building permits in 2025

The county's population peaked at 1,721,300 in 1970 and has fallen in each census since. A county-wide figure hides large differences between Cleveland, the inner ring and the outer suburbs, so price a particular house from comparable sales or a written offer.

When is Cuyahoga County real estate tax due?

Mid-February and mid-August, according to the Treasurer's Pay Your Taxes page. The tax is billed in arrears, so taxes accrued in 2025 are payable in 2026.

When can I file a valuation complaint in Cuyahoga County?

January 1 through March 31. The Board of Revision says the next filing period is January 1, 2027 through March 31, 2027.

Is there a fee to pay my Cuyahoga County tax online?

Not for an electronic check. A debit card costs a flat $2.95 and a credit card costs 2.3% with a minimum of $1.50.

What penalty applies to a late real estate tax payment?

ORC 323.121 sets a ten percent penalty on the unpaid half, cut in half if the whole amount is paid within ten days. Interest is charged on delinquent taxes as well.

Can the county help if I cannot pay all at once?

Yes. The Treasurer lists a delinquent tax payment plan page and holds Last Chance Payment Plan classes for owners seeking a third contract. Call the Treasurer's Office to ask which plan fits.

Franklin County by the numbers

Who runs property tax in Franklin County?

Three offices split the job. The Franklin County Auditor appraises each parcel and keeps ownership records. The Treasurer sends the bills and takes the payments. The Board of Revision listens to value disputes. Knowing which one owns your question saves phone calls.

  • Auditor: 373 S. High Street, 21st floor, Columbus; phone 614-525-4663. Handles property values, homestead applications, transfers and the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program.
  • Treasurer: 373 South High Street, 17th floor; phone 614-525-3438; weekday counter hours run from 8 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon Handles bills, payments, payment plans and the budget payment program.
  • Board of Revision: phone 614-525-3913, email BOR@franklincountyohio.gov. Hears complaints about appraised value.

The Auditor's real estate division oversees the appraisal of 483,319 parcels and processes more than $2 billion in tax collections for more than 85 entities countywide.

When are Franklin County property taxes due?

Owners can pay the annual bill in one installment early in the year, in two installments, or in monthly installments. The Treasurer posts the 2026 collection dates as follows.

PaymentDate posted by the Treasurer
First half, 2026 collectionFebruary 28, 2026 on the Collection Dates page; March 2, 2026 on the Real Estate Taxes page
Second half, 2026 collectionJuly 20, 2026
Penalty and interestApply to taxes paid after the due date; a missing bill does not avoid them

Source: Franklin County Treasurer. The first-half date moved in 2026, so read the date printed on your own bill instead of an older calendar. Both 2026 dates have passed. Ohio puts the duty on the parcel owner to get a bill in time to pay, and the Treasurer will send a duplicate by phone or online request at 614-525-3438.

Property taxes are billed in arrears and can be paid only after the Auditor assesses them. The Budget Payment Program lets you prepay monthly into an escrow account in your name, which is applied automatically when the semi-annual bill comes due. Under Ohio Revised Code 7.16, the county posts its full tax rate listing on the Columbus Dispatch website.

Mailed payments go to the Franklin County Treasurer with the parcel number and a daytime phone number written on the check, along with the billing statement. Enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself if you want a receipt. The office has a kiosk for credit card payments through its secure payment site. When a payment is returned, the Treasurer reverses it after the bank notifies the office, which normally takes two to three business days, and charges no returned item fee, although a penalty can still apply if the due date is missed.

How does Franklin County value my house?

Ohio law requires a reappraisal of all real property every six years, with an update at the three-year midpoint. Franklin County completed its countywide reappraisal in 2023 and a triennial update in 2026.

Between those cycles the Treasurer says a value changes only for three reasons:

  • physical changes such as a new porch, patio or deck
  • demolition of a structure
  • a Board of Revision decision on a filed complaint

A bill equals the tax rate times the value of the property, so a lower value flows straight to the bill. On the Treasurer's property search, the Distribution tab shows how your bill splits among the school district, municipality, library and other entities.

Where can I contest a Franklin County property value?

Complaints about value start with the Board of Revision. For tax year 2026, the Treasurer's FAQ says the Auditor's office accepts valuation complaints from November 20, 2026 until March 31, 2027, and the Board of Revision page confirms the March 31, 2027 end. The tax year 2025 window has already closed.

The Board of Revision reviews the Auditor's appraised value and can change it based on evidence. Useful documents include a closing statement, a purchase contract or an appraisal. Hearings are held by Zoom, and an in-person hearing can be requested at least 10 days ahead. Some cases go to mediation, which is less formal. The Board hears complaints about value, so the tax dollars you pay and the rate are outside its authority.

A party unhappy with the ruling has 30 days from the date it was mailed to file a notice of appeal with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or with the Court of Common Pleas. The notice must also go to the Board of Revision, and to the County Auditor for a court filing.

What tax relief does Franklin County offer?

The Auditor and Treasurer list several programs, each with its own application:

  • Homestead exemption: for owners who turn 65 by the end of the application year, or totally and permanently disabled as of January 1, living in the home as a primary residence. The Auditor's page cites a total income limit of $41,000 for applications tied to a 2025 return. Applications go to Franklin County Auditor, Homestead, 373 S High St, 21st Floor, or to homestead@franklincountyohio.gov.
  • Enhanced homestead exemption: for veterans who are 100% disabled from service-connected injuries and for surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty. No income test applies, and approval reduces taxes on $50,000 of appraised value.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation (CAUV): farmland valued by soil type. Applications and renewals are due the first Monday of March.
  • Penalty remission: file form 23-A with the Treasurer's Office to ask that a late-payment penalty be forgiven.
  • Delinquent tax payment plans: the Treasurer offers plans to bring a past due account current.

Around 40,000 Franklin County parcels receive some tax incentive such as an abatement or a tax increment financing arrangement.

How does a sale change my Franklin County tax situation?

Ownership changes pass through the Auditor ahead of the Recorder, and the county's conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price unless the seller is receiving the homestead exemption, in which case it is $1 per $1,000. Franklin County's transfer charge is $0.50 on every non-exempt transfer.

Ohio law requires the buyer's statement of value to say whether the seller reported a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the home and whether the land was in farm use valuation (R.C. 319.202). When a reduction exists, buyer and seller account for the estimated amount between them. A farm use property that leaves the program can face a recoupment charge.

Because bills arrive in arrears, the closing statement is where a seller and buyer divide the year. Ask the title agent for the current payment status from the Treasurer's property search, and ask the Treasurer about any penalty remission before closing. A seller behind on payments can ask the Treasurer about a delinquent payment plan.

What should I know about Franklin County?

Franklin County was established April 30, 1803 and covers about 544 square miles. Columbus is the county seat. The 2020 census counted 1,323,807 people, the most of any Ohio county, and 540,369 households. The county is the center of the Columbus metropolitan area and borders Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties.

Property in a city such as Dublin, Gahanna, Hilliard or Westerville is billed by the same county Treasurer, but the tax rate depends on the taxing districts that cover the parcel, such as the school district and municipality.

Where do I file a Franklin County property value complaint?

With the Board of Revision through the Auditor's office. Tax year 2026 complaints are accepted from November 20, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

Which Franklin County office answers questions about a tax bill?

The Treasurer at 614-525-3438. Value questions go to the Auditor at 614-525-4663, and complaints go to the Board of Revision at 614-525-3913.

Can I pay Franklin County property taxes monthly?

Yes. The Treasurer allows monthly installments and runs a Budget Payment Program that holds prepayments in an escrow account in your name and applies them to the bill.

Is the Franklin County conveyance fee lower for homestead sellers?

Yes. The Auditor's calculator lowers the conveyance fee from $3 to $1 per $1,000 of the sale price when the seller receives the homestead exemption at the time of transfer.

Who sets and collects property tax in Geauga County?

Sitting on the Board of Revision are the Auditor, its permanent secretary, the president of the County Commissioners and the Treasurer. The Auditor's office is at 231 Main Street, Suite 1-A, Chardon, Ohio 44024, with a real estate direct line of (440) 279-1617 and a main line of (440) 279-1600.

When are Geauga County property taxes billed and due?

Bills for the first half are issued in January and for the second half in June. The Auditor's property search page says the payment deadlines fall on the second Wednesday in February and the second Wednesday in July.

The Treasurer sends tax bills only by regular mail, and the Auditor's portal warns that any text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent. The portal also carries a yearly tax calendar for the exact dates.

  • Any text asking you to pay is a scam, so delete it.

How many parcels does the Geauga County Auditor value?

On January 1, 2026 the Auditor's portal counted 52,207 parcels in Geauga County. The Auditor's real estate page says the office must see that every parcel and the buildings on it are fairly and uniformly appraised.

How often are Geauga County values updated?

State law has every parcel reappraised at six-year intervals, with a mid-cycle update in year three. The Auditor's appraisal office carries out the sexennial reappraisals, the triennial updates and annual new construction valuations, and its field appraisers visit every property that was issued a building or zoning permit during the year.

The Auditor's portal has posted tentative values for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, for owners to search by parcel. The appraisal page lists what changes a value: added square footage, additions, new outbuildings and major improvements that needed a permit. New carpet, appliances, fixtures, landscaping and a new driveway surface do not.

What is the process to dispute my Geauga County valuation?

Begin by asking one of the Auditor's appraisers for an informal review. If you still disagree, a formal complaint goes to the Board of Revision, and the appraisal office wants solid evidence for at least one of these three grounds.

  • The record describes the property wrongly, for instance a carport listed as a garage.
  • The estimate runs above what comparable homes sold for, or above a bank appraisal.
  • Your value is out of line with the estimates on similar homes nearby.

R.C. 5715.19 gives owners until the end of March after the tax year, or until first-half collection closes if that falls later. The Board then has 180 days from the final filing date to rule. A parcel already challenged during the same interim period cannot be challenged again unless it sold at arm's length, lost value to casualty or gained a major improvement.

What tax relief does Geauga County offer homeowners?

The Homestead Exemption shields $29,000 of a home's market value from local taxes, and the Auditor's page puts the average Geauga savings at about $518 a year. The Auditor's own example is that a $100,000 home would be billed as if it were worth $71,000.

  • Seniors: turn 65 by the end of 2026 and keep household income below $41,000, measured as 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income.
  • Disabled owners: certified permanently and totally disabled on January 1, 2026, under the same income cap.
  • Veterans: hold a total (100 percent) service-connected rating and file form DTE 105I.
  • Surviving spouses: of someone who was getting the old exemption, if at least 59 when the spouse died.

File a paper application, DTE 105A, with the Auditor by December 31. The signature must be original, and the office does not accept electronic filing. If the Auditor denies you, form DTE 106B carries the appeal to the Board of Revision. The Auditor also runs an Owner Occupancy Credit tool, the farm CAUV and forestry programs and a destroyed property deduction.

What if a Geauga County house is damaged or destroyed?

The Auditor can lower the value of real estate hurt by fire, flood, ice or other causes, but cannot issue refunds for earlier years. File the damaged property application as soon as possible. The deduction depends on the calendar quarter of the damage.

Damage from January through March earns a 100 percent deduction and April through June earns 75 percent, and the deadline for both is December 31. July through September earns 50 percent with the same deadline. October through December earns 25 percent, with a January 31 deadline. The reduction stays until the property is restored.

How do taxes play out at a Geauga County closing?

Geauga County deeds go to the Auditor for transfer before they are recorded. At the Auditor the fees are $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value plus $0.50 per parcel, and the tax records are updated as the parcel changes hands.

Get the balance on the parcel from the Treasurer, then confirm with your title company who pays the February and July installments. The Auditor's real estate page also links a Forfeited Land Sale page, which is the place to look if taxes on a parcel were missed.

What do Geauga County's housing statistics show?

The 2020 Census counted 95,397 people in Geauga County. Owners occupy 87.2 percent of the housing stock, the median home they own is worth $331,100, and the median household earns $107,860. The county issued 180 building permits in 2025.

Geauga dates to 1806 and spans about 400 square miles of land. Its municipalities include Chardon, Burton, Middlefield and South Russell, and a November 2024 vote dissolved the Village of Aquilla.

More questions about Geauga County, OH Property Tax Guide

When are Geauga County property taxes due?

The second Wednesday in February covers the first half and the second Wednesday in July covers the second half. The Treasurer mails the bills ahead of each date, in January and June.

How much can the Geauga County homestead exemption save?

The exemption shields $29,000 of market value, and the Auditor estimates average savings of about $518 a year. You must apply on paper with the Auditor by December 31 and meet the age or disability and income rules.

Where does a Geauga County value dispute start?

Ask the Auditor's appraisal office for an informal review first. If that fails, a complaint to the Board of Revision must reach the Auditor by the end of the following March, or when first-half collection closes if that is later.

Will the Geauga County Treasurer text me a tax bill?

No. The Treasurer sends bills only by regular mail. A text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent and should be deleted.

Which number reaches the Geauga County real estate tax staff?

Questions about values, exemptions and credits go to the Auditor's real estate line, (440) 279-1617. The main Auditor number is (440) 279-1600, answered on weekdays between 8:00 and 4:30.

Owners live in 65% of occupied homes and renters in 35%. The median home was built in 1978, about 45 years ago.
